cases.abstract: FlashAttention avoids quadratic attention intermediates in GPU memory, but reducing those transfers still leaves arithmetic and scheduling costs that limit throughput. FlashAttention-2 addresses these costs while preserving exact attention. It delays softmax normalization until all key tiles have been processed, reducing non-matrix arithmetic that is expensive relative to tensor-core operations. It also assigns independent query blocks to separate thread blocks and distinct query rows to warps, increasing available parallelism while removing forward inter-warp reductions. The computation remains quadratic in sequence length, with linear auxiliary storage. In A100 80GB benchmarks spanning sequences of 512 to 16k tokens at a fixed total of 16k tokens, FlashAttention-2 is 1.7-3.0 times faster than FlashAttention and reaches a reported peak of 230 TFLOPs/s. For GPT-style models with 1.3B or 2.7B parameters trained on eight A100 GPUs, throughput increases by up to 1.3 times relative to FlashAttention, with larger gains at 8k than at 2k context. These comparisons show that better execution of unchanged attention yields a workload-dependent training benefit, rather than the full kernel-level acceleration.
cases.methods: FlashAttention-2 retains tiled online softmax but removes repeated division of partial outputs by the running normalization constant. For each query tile, it accumulates an exponential sum and an unnormalized, exponentially weighted sum of values across key tiles. If a new tile raises the row maximum, both accumulators are rescaled to the new reference before incorporating that tile; only the final output is normalized. This preserves the attention result while reducing scalar work that cannot exploit the GPU's fast matrix-multiplication units. Saved row-wise log-sum-exp statistics let the backward pass reconstruct probabilities without storing the attention matrix. Independent query tiles also provide parallel work when batch and head counts are small. Within each thread block, assigning separate query rows to warps avoids a forward reduction across key partitions. Larger tiles can reduce shared-memory traffic, but register spilling or shared-memory exhaustion limits this choice.
cases.results: Longer contexts yield substantially larger training gains than shorter ones in the tested GPT-style models. On eight A100 80GB GPUs, FlashAttention-2 raises throughput for the 1.3B-parameter model from 189 to 196 TFLOPs/s per GPU at 2k context, compared with 170 to 220 at 8k, relative to FlashAttention. The 2.7B model follows the same pattern, reaching 225 rather than 175 TFLOPs/s at 8k. Thus the attention optimization delivers roughly 1.3-fold training speedups at 8k, but the much smaller 2k improvement shows that kernel acceleration does not transfer uniformly to full-model throughput. These figures use the paper's model-FLOP convention, which counts attention without halving FLOPs for causal masking. Attention-only benchmarks provide a complementary memory result: with 16k total tokens, FlashAttention-2 runs at 16k sequence length where standard PyTorch attention exhausts memory. The training and kernel comparisons therefore establish different benefits: faster complete training in the tested long-context settings and attention execution without quadratic intermediate storage.
cases.notes: The retained promises map to exact tiled computation and linear auxiliary storage in Section 3.1, kernel acceleration in Section 4.1, and complete-training throughput in Table 1. The context comparison tests the application-level benefit without isolating individual implementation changes. The reported 230 TFLOPs/s is a kernel maximum; Table 1 uses its stated causal-attention FLOP convention. Exactness concerns the mathematical operation, not bitwise identity. H100-specific gains proposed as future work are not treated as measurements.

cases.abstract: Autoregressive generation makes serial calls to a large model even when hardware has capacity to evaluate several continuations together. Speculative decoding uses that capacity to reduce latency while preserving the target model's output distribution. A cheap draft model proposes tokens sequentially, and the target evaluates their prefixes in parallel. Probability-based acceptance retains a valid prefix; a residual distribution corrects the first rejection, or full acceptance allows one additional target token. The correction guarantees distributional equivalence for any draft model, whereas acceleration depends on both draft cost and agreement with the target. Under independent, identically distributed acceptance rates and unchanged target latency during concurrent evaluation, the analysis relates these quantities to progress per iteration and expected speedup. On a single TPU-v4 at batch size one, a 77M-parameter T5 draft accelerates the 11B-parameter T5-XXL model by 3.4 times for greedy translation and 2.6 times for standard sampling; summarization gains are 3.1 and 2.3 times, respectively. Larger drafts accept more proposals but yield smaller speedups in these tests. Its latency gains trade increased arithmetic for fewer serial target steps and require computational capacity for concurrent evaluation.
cases.methods: For the chosen sampling rule, let p and q be the target and draft token distributions. Accepting a draft token x with probability min(1,p(x)/q(x)) assigns accepted mass min(p(x),q(x)); sampling after rejection from the normalized positive part of p-q supplies the missing mass. Their sum recovers p for any draft distribution, independently of the assumptions used to predict speed. The draft generates gamma proposals sequentially, and the target checks gamma+1 prefixes in parallel. Only the accepted prefix is retained, followed by a correction token or an additional target token after full acceptance. If acceptance rates across prefixes are independent and identically distributed with mean alpha, expected progress is (1-alpha^(gamma+1))/(1-alpha) tokens per iteration. Dividing by 1+gamma*c, where c is the draft-to-target runtime ratio, predicts walltime speedup for sufficiently long generations when concurrent target evaluations add no latency.
cases.results: Better draft agreement does not necessarily produce faster decoding. For greedy English-to-German translation with seven proposals per iteration, T5-large achieves mean acceptance of 0.82 but only a 1.7-fold speedup, whereas T5-small reaches 0.75 acceptance and a 3.4-fold speedup. Both use the same 11B-parameter T5-XXL target, batch size one, and a single TPU-v4. The smaller draft's advantage despite lower acceptance supports selecting a draft by its cost-acceptance balance rather than agreement alone. Sampling also changes the payoff: T5-small's translation speedup falls to 2.6-fold at temperature one, while its summarization speedup falls from 3.1-fold under greedy decoding to 2.3-fold at temperature one. The proposal counts remain seven for translation and five for summarization in these comparisons. Rejected proposals leave some target evaluations unused, so these walltime gains are not arithmetic savings. They depend on spare computation for concurrent verification, rather than providing an acceleration for configurations already limited by available compute.
cases.notes: The exactness claim rests on speculative sampling, not on the independent-acceptance approximation used for speed predictions. Table 2 tests the cost-acceptance tradeoff through T5 draft comparisons; its temperature comparisons retain the T5-small proposal counts. Walltime evidence is confined to T5 at batch size one on a single TPU-v4. GPT-like and LaMDA measurements concern acceptance rates only. Distributional equivalence does not require identical sampled sequences, and adaptive proposal counts, beam search, and non-text applications remain unvalidated here.
